content.comment_body: I'm working on creating a custom control program where an on/off delay relay should keep an output active when an input signal is switched off and quickly back on. My current implementation resets the Q2 and Q3 outputs whenever their inputs cycle, but I need them to remain on if the input interruption is shorter than the off delay period. Does anyone have suggestions? I've spent several days troubleshooting this seemingly simple switching logic. Note: The attached file is not a ZIP; the extension was just changed from .lsc.
Please give this solution a try. If it doesn't work, feel free to report back.

I've already attempted that configuration, but it causes an undesired effect: it pulses the output unnecessarily, leading to increased equipment wear. In this setup, even a very brief input signal causes the output to activate momentarily. What I need is for the output to remain off unless the input stays on for the full one-second duration. It would be much easier if the on/off delay function behaved like a physical relay, maintaining a closed circuit unless the input is disabled for the full delay period.
Hello [user_name], Check the attachment for my approach to your issue. I hope this meets your requirements! Best regards [user_name]

Thank you, this solved my problem! I wasn't aware of the "Invert connector" feature, which initially confused me since the relays you added behaved differently. Learning about this will help me with future projects too. Thanks again!

analysis.insight_summary: Users struggled to configure an on/off delay relay to keep outputs active during short interruptions in input, aiming for logic that mimics physical relays. The main usability challenge was the complexity of timer settings, which led to unintended output pulsing and potential equipment wear. Discovering the 'Invert connector' feature was essential for achieving the desired control behavior.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expected the delay relay logic to maintain output states during brief input interruptions, similar to the function of physical relays. They sought intuitive and reliable timer controls that avoid unnecessary pulsing.
